 Dated this the 11th day of January 2016
 O R D E R

The accused in S.T.No.1762 of 1997 on the files of the Court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class,
Chalakudy filed this Revision Petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 2(ia)(a)(m) and 7(i) read with Section 16(1)(a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and Rule 5 Appendix B.A.17.11 of Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955.

entities.text:
Judicial Magistrate of First Class,
Chalakudy
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
2. Heard.
3.
The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:-
On 7.11.1996 at 3 p.m., PW2, the Food Inspector, purchased 375 gram of gingelly oil from the shop of the revision petitioner.
After sampling as per rules, one of the samples was sent for analysis to the Public Analyst.

The Public Analyst filed Ext. P3 report stating that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for gingelly oil under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1956 and therefore, the same was adulterated.
Thereafter, on the request of the accused, the second sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis.
Ext.P6 certificate of the Central Food Laboratory would show that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for gingelly oil and therefore, it was adulterated.
4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW3 were examined and Exts. P1 to P17 were marked for the prosecution.
No evidence was adduced on the side of the revision petitioner.

5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext. P6 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated.
The learned counsel for the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.

entities.text: Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was prescribed as mandated under Section 23 (1-A)
(ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.

Therefore, Ext. P6 certificate of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra).

It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra)
that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal.

In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court M.V.Thomas vs Food Inspector on 11 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/49636624/
2 acquitted the accused.
The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor.

Even otherwise, in view of the decision in Pepsico India Holdings (supra), the conviction in this case cannot be sustained as no laboratory was notified and no validated method of analysis was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

In the result, this Revision Petition stands allowed setting aside the conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sec.2(ia)(a)(m) and 7(i) read with Section 16(1)(a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and Rule 5 Appendix B.A.17.11 of Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 and the revision petitioner is acquitted for the said offence.
The bail bond of the revision petitioner stands cancelled and he is set at liberty.

Sd/-
B.SUDHEENDRA KUMAR, JUDGE dl/.20.1..2016 // True Copy // PA to Judge M.V.Thomas vs Food Inspector on 11 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/49636624/
